source.title: The Constitution of India (original question writing)

chapter.name: Fundamental Rights: Your Claim Against the State
chapter.blurb: The idea and list of fundamental rights, equality, freedoms, rights against exploitation and of religion, constitutional remedies, and the limits and amendment of rights.

concepts.name: What fundamental rights are
concepts.description: The idea of enforceable rights against the State, where they sit in the Constitution and how a law that breaks them is treated.
concepts.idea: Fundamental rights are guarantees in Part III that a citizen can enforce in court against the State.
concepts.rule: Part III of the Constitution (Articles 12 to 35) lists the fundamental rights. Article 12 says who counts as 'the State': the Union and State governments, Parliament and the legislatures, and local and other authorities. Article 13 makes any law that takes away or waters down these rights void to that extent. The rights are justiciable, so a person whose right is violated can go straight to the Supreme Court under Article 32. They are not absolute: the State may impose reasonable restrictions in the public interest. The right to property was removed from this list by the 44th Amendment (1978) and now survives as an ordinary legal right in Article 300A.
concepts.example: A person whose house is demolished by a municipal body without notice can question the action as an act of 'the State'.

questions.q: Fundamental rights are found in Part ____ of the Constitution.
questions.a: III

questions.q: The articles that make up the fundamental rights run from
questions.a: Article 12 to Article 35

questions.q: The definition of 'the State' for this Part is given in
questions.a: Article 12

questions.q: The right to property is today protected as a legal right under
questions.a: Article 300A

questions.q: What does it mean to say fundamental rights are justiciable?
questions.a: A court can enforce them when they are violated
o: A court can enforce them when they are violated
They can be changed by any ordinary law
They apply only in times of war
They are only advice to the government

questions.q: A law that goes against a fundamental right is declared ____ to that extent under Article 13.
questions.a: void

questions.q: Fundamental rights are mainly available against
questions.a: the State and its authorities

questions.q: Why is the phrase 'reasonable restrictions' attached to several rights?
questions.a: Rights have to be balanced with public order and the rights of others
o: Rights have to be balanced with public order and the rights of others
Rights are meant to be withdrawn every year
Only officials may decide who has rights
The Constitution wants rights to be unusable

questions.q: Which is a correct description of Article 13?
questions.a: It voids laws that conflict with fundamental rights
o: It voids laws that conflict with fundamental rights
It lists the duties of a citizen
It fixes the term of the Lok Sabha

questions.q: A state-run university refuses admission on an unfair ground. Whom is the student complaining against?
questions.a: The State, as the university is a public authority
o: The State, as the university is a public authority
No one, as rights cannot be enforced

questions.q: A state law takes away the freedom to form associations without a fair reason. The law is
questions.a: open to being struck down by a court
o: open to being struck down by a court

questions.q: A citizen's fundamental right is violated by a police officer. Name the authority she can approach directly and the Article that allows it.
questions.a: She can approach the Supreme Court directly under Article 32.

questions.q: Explain why a shopkeeper cannot ordinarily sue his neighbour for violating Article 19.
questions.a: Fundamental rights are mainly enforced against the State and its authorities, not against private individuals.

questions.q: After 1978 a person whose land is acquired by the government would claim compensation under
questions.a: Article 300A as a legal right

questions.q: Explain how Articles 12, 13 and 32 work together to protect a citizen against an unfair law.
questions.a: Article 12 identifies the State whose actions are checked, Article 13 makes an inconsistent law void, and Article 32 lets the citizen go to the Supreme Court for a remedy.

questions.q: Which statement best captures why rights are placed in a written Constitution?
questions.a: They cannot be taken away by a simple majority in the legislature
o: They cannot be taken away by a simple majority in the legislature
They are easy to change every year
They apply only to the government
They are meant for judges alone

questions.q: Compare a fundamental right with an ordinary legal right such as the one in Article 300A.
questions.a: A fundamental right is guaranteed in Part III and enforced directly through Article 32, while an ordinary legal right is created by law and enforced through the usual courts and can be regulated by legislation.

questions.q: Why did the removal of the right to property from Part III not leave owners without any protection?
questions.a: Article 300A still says no person shall be deprived of property except by authority of law, so acquisition needs a valid law even though it is no longer a fundamental right.

questions.q: 'Rights that can be enforced in court are stronger than rights that are only promised.' Do you agree? Give one reason.
questions.a: Yes, since a justiciable right gives a remedy against violation; a reasoned answer is accepted.

questions.q: Draw a simple chart showing how a citizen moves from a violated right to a remedy, naming three steps.
questions.a: Rights violated by the State, petition to the court under Article 32 or Article 226, and the court orders a remedy or strikes down the law.

concepts.name: Equality before the law
concepts.description: Articles 14 to 18: equal protection, no discrimination, equal opportunity in public jobs, ending untouchability and titles.
concepts.idea: The State must treat people alike and cannot use birth or status to give some people advantage.
concepts.rule: Article 14 promises equality before the law and equal protection of the laws. Article 15 forbids discrimination on grounds only of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth, though special provisions for women, children and weaker sections are allowed. Article 16 guarantees equality of opportunity in public employment, with provision for reservation. Article 17 abolishes untouchability and makes its practice punishable. Article 18 abolishes titles, except military and academic distinctions, and stops a citizen from accepting titles from a foreign State.
concepts.example: A government job advertisement cannot be limited to men of one caste without a permitted reason.

questions.q: Untouchability is abolished by Article ____.
Equality before the law is promised by
questions.a: Article 14

questions.q: Equality of opportunity in public employment is found in
questions.a: Article 16

questions.q: Under Article 18 the State may confer
questions.a: military and academic distinctions

questions.q: What does 'equal protection of the laws' mean?
questions.a: People in like situations are treated alike
o: People in like situations are treated alike
Everyone must be given identical benefits
Only citizens may go to court
Laws are the same in every country

questions.q: Article 15 bars discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of ____.
questions.a: birth

questions.q: Article 17 makes the practice of untouchability
questions.a: a punishable offence

questions.q: Why does Article 15 still allow special provisions for women and children?
questions.a: Equality can require special care for those who start with a disadvantage
o: Equality can require special care for those who start with a disadvantage
It applies only to citizens of large cities

questions.q: Which is true about Article 14?
questions.a: It applies to citizens and to other persons within India
o: It applies to citizens and to other persons within India
It applies only to government servants

questions.q: A shop refuses entry to a person because of his caste. Which Article is most directly relevant?
questions.a: Article 15

questions.q: A public post is closed to women for no valid reason. This offends
questions.a: Article 16

questions.q: A village bars a family from the common well because of their caste. Which Article is broken and why?
questions.a: Article 17, since untouchability is abolished and its practice in any form is forbidden.

questions.q: A university awards a gold medal for academic merit. Does this break Article 18? Explain.
questions.a: No, because academic distinctions are an exception to the abolition of titles.

questions.q: A citizen is offered a title by a foreign government. Under Article 18 he
questions.a: may not accept it without the consent of the President
o: may not accept it without the consent of the President
must return it within a year
must give it to the Prime Minister

questions.q: A law reserves some seats for women in a local body. Argue whether this is consistent with the equality Articles.
questions.a: It is consistent, because Article 15 allows special provisions for women and the aim is real equality of participation, not discrimination.

questions.q: How does Article 16 differ from Article 15?
questions.a: Article 16 is about public employment while Article 15 is about wider access such as shops and wells
o: Article 16 is about public employment while Article 15 is about wider access such as shops and wells

questions.q: Distinguish between formal equality and equality that needs special provisions, using Article 15 as an example.
questions.a: Formal equality treats everyone identically, while Article 15 allows special provisions for women, children and weaker sections to make equality real.

questions.q: Explain how Articles 14 to 18 together seek to end social hierarchy.
questions.a: Article 14 gives equal law, Article 15 bars discrimination, Article 16 opens jobs on merit, Article 17 ends untouchability and Article 18 ends hereditary titles, so birth cannot decide status.

questions.q: Is reservation in public jobs against the promise of equal opportunity? Give your view with one reason.
questions.a: A reasoned view is accepted, for example that it is allowed by Article 16 to correct historical disadvantage.

questions.q: Design a poster with one slogan for each of Articles 14, 15, 16, 17 and 18.
questions.a: A poster with five short slogans, each matched to its Article correctly.

concepts.name: Freedoms and protection of life and liberty
concepts.description: Articles 19 to 22: the six freedoms, safeguards for accused persons, the right to life and personal liberty, education and arrest.
concepts.idea: Citizens enjoy specific freedoms, and life, liberty and fair procedure are protected against arbitrary State action.
concepts.rule: Article 19(1) gives citizens six freedoms: speech and expression; assembling peaceably without arms; forming associations, unions or cooperative societies; moving freely throughout India; residing and settling in any part; and practising any profession or carrying on any trade. Each can be limited by reasonable restrictions. Article 20 protects an accused against a law applied backwards, against being punished twice for the same offence and against being forced to testify against oneself. Article 21 says no person shall be deprived of life or personal liberty except by procedure established by law. Article 21A (86th Amendment, 2002) makes education free and compulsory for children aged 6 to 14. Article 22 gives safeguards on arrest, including being told the grounds and being produced before a magistrate within 24 hours.
concepts.example: A person arrested must be taken before a magistrate within 24 hours, excluding travel time.

questions.q: Freedom of speech and expression is in Article ____ (1)(a).
Life and personal liberty are protected by
questions.a: Article 21

questions.q: An arrested person must be produced before a magistrate within
questions.a: 24 hours

questions.q: The right to education for children aged 6 to 14 was inserted by the
questions.a: 86th Amendment

questions.q: Article 19(1) freedoms are available to
questions.a: citizens

questions.q: Article 20 protects a person from being punished twice for the same offence, which is called protection against double ____.
questions.a: jeopardy

questions.q: What does the right against self-incrimination mean?
questions.a: An accused cannot be forced to be a witness against himself
o: An accused cannot be forced to be a witness against himself
An accused must confess to the court
A witness may not speak to the police
A judge must punish the accused

questions.q: Why must reasonable restrictions accompany freedom of speech?
questions.a: Speech may harm public order, decency or others' reputation
o: Speech may harm public order, decency or others' reputation
Speech is not important in a democracy

questions.q: Which is a freedom under Article 19(1)?
questions.a: To move freely throughout the territory of India
o: To move freely throughout the territory of India
To be exempt from all taxes

questions.q: A protest march held peacefully and without arms relies on the freedom to
questions.a: assemble peaceably

questions.q: A person is punished under a law made after the act was done. Which protection is broken?
questions.a: Article 20 protection against ex post facto laws
o: Article 20 protection against ex post facto laws

questions.q: A man is arrested and kept in custody for three days without being produced before a magistrate. Which safeguard is broken and under which Article?
questions.a: The 24-hour production rule of Article 22 is broken.

questions.q: A newspaper is stopped from printing an article critical of the government without any legal ground. Which freedom is affected and can the State restrict it in any way?
questions.a: Freedom of speech and expression in Article 19(1)(a); it can be restricted only by reasonable restrictions on permitted grounds, not arbitrarily.

questions.q: A child aged 8 is denied a place in school. Which provision is most relevant?
questions.a: Article 21A

questions.q: Explain how Articles 20, 21 and 22 together shield a person accused of a crime.
questions.a: Article 20 limits how the law can punish him, Article 21 requires fair procedure before liberty is lost, and Article 22 gives safeguards such as being told the grounds of arrest and going before a magistrate in 24 hours.

questions.q: Why is Article 21 considered a wide provision?
questions.a: Courts have read it to include dignity, health and fair procedure
o: Courts have read it to include dignity, health and fair procedure
It applies only to the arrested
It has no limits at all

questions.q: Compare the freedom to assemble under Article 19 with the freedom of a person to be free from arbitrary arrest under Article 22.
questions.a: Article 19 protects a collective activity such as peaceful assembly, whereas Article 22 protects an individual's liberty against arbitrary arrest and detention.

questions.q: Why are the six freedoms of Article 19 not absolute, and what balance does the Constitution aim for?
questions.a: The State can apply reasonable restrictions in the interest of public order, security of the State, morality and others' rights, so individual liberty is balanced with the wider good.

questions.q: Should freedom of speech ever be restricted? Give one reason for your answer.
questions.a: A reasoned answer is accepted, such as that it may be restricted to prevent violence but not to silence criticism.

questions.q: Create a short case study of an arrest in which three safeguards of Article 22 are followed.
questions.a: A case in which the person is told the grounds, allowed to consult a lawyer, and produced before a magistrate within 24 hours.

concepts.name: Rights against exploitation, of religion and of minorities
concepts.description: Articles 23 to 30: bans on forced labour and child labour, freedom of religion, and cultural and educational rights.
concepts.idea: Articles 23 to 30 protect people from exploitation and protect religious and cultural freedoms.
concepts.rule: Article 23 prohibits human trafficking and forced labour (begar). Article 24 forbids employing children below 14 in factories, mines or other hazardous work. Article 25 gives every person freedom of conscience and the right to profess, practise and propagate religion, subject to public order, morality and health. Article 26 lets religious denominations manage their own religious affairs. Article 27 says no one can be compelled to pay taxes for promoting a particular religion. Article 28 restricts religious instruction in institutions wholly maintained by the State. Article 29 protects the language, script and culture of any section of citizens, and Article 30 gives religious and linguistic minorities the right to establish and administer educational institutions of their choice.
concepts.example: A factory cannot employ a 12-year-old to work on hazardous machinery.

questions.q: Forced labour is banned by Article ____.
Employment of children below 14 in hazardous work is prohibited by
questions.a: Article 24

questions.q: Freedom of conscience and religion is given by
questions.a: Article 25

questions.q: The right of minorities to run educational institutions is in
questions.a: Article 30

questions.q: What is 'begar'?
questions.a: Unpaid forced labour

questions.q: Article 26 lets religious denominations manage their own religious ____.
questions.a: affairs

questions.q: Article 27 protects a person from
questions.a: being taxed to promote a particular religion
o: being taxed to promote a particular religion

questions.q: Why is the freedom of religion in Article 25 made subject to public order, morality and health?
questions.a: Religious practice must not harm others or society
o: Religious practice must not harm others or society

questions.q: Which best describes Article 29?
questions.a: It protects the language, script and culture of sections of citizens
o: It protects the language, script and culture of sections of citizens
It bans all schools of a religion
It sets up the Supreme Court

questions.q: A child of 10 is made to work in a mine. Which Article is broken?
questions.a: Article 24

questions.q: A group of villagers is forced to work without wages. Which Article applies?
questions.a: Article 23

questions.q: A linguistic minority wants to open a school in its own language. Which Article helps it and what does it allow?
questions.a: Article 30, which lets minorities establish and administer educational institutions of their choice.

questions.q: A State-run school compels all pupils to attend prayers of one religion. Which Article is relevant and why?
questions.a: Article 28, since religious instruction in State-maintained institutions is restricted and no one can be forced to attend it.

questions.q: A temple trust decides whom to appoint as its priest under its own custom. Which Article protects this?
questions.a: Article 26, within limits of public order, morality and health
o: Article 26, within limits of public order, morality and health

questions.q: Explain how Article 25 and Article 26 differ in whom they protect.
questions.a: Article 25 protects each individual's freedom of conscience and religion, while Article 26 protects religious denominations' right to manage their own religious affairs.

questions.q: Which statement links Articles 29 and 30?
questions.a: Article 29 protects culture and Article 30 gives institutions to preserve it
o: Article 29 protects culture and Article 30 gives institutions to preserve it
They apply only to the majority

questions.q: Compare freedom of religion with freedom from exploitation as protections.
questions.a: Freedom of religion (Articles 25-28) protects belief and practice, while the rights against exploitation (Articles 23-24) protect the bodily and economic dignity of the person.

questions.q: Explain why the Constitution protects both individual and group rights in the field of religion and culture.
questions.a: Individuals need freedom of conscience, while communities need to keep their institutions and culture, so Articles 25 to 30 secure both.

questions.q: Should there be a limit on religious practice in the interest of public health? Give your view and one reason.
questions.a: A reasoned view is accepted, as Article 25 itself allows restrictions on public order, morality and health.

questions.q: Prepare a table matching Articles 23 to 30 with their subjects in one line each.
questions.a: A table with the Article number and the subject: 23 forced labour, 24 child labour, 25 religion, 26 religious affairs, 27 religious taxes, 28 religious instruction, 29 culture, 30 minority institutions.

concepts.name: Constitutional remedies and writs
concepts.description: Article 32, Article 226, the five writs and the special status of the right to move the courts.
concepts.idea: Article 32 makes the right to move the Supreme Court a fundamental right, and the courts issue writs to enforce rights.
concepts.rule: Article 32 lets a person go directly to the Supreme Court to enforce a fundamental right, and Dr Ambedkar called it the heart and soul of the Constitution. High Courts have a similar and wider power under Article 226, which can also be used for purposes other than fundamental rights. The five writs are habeas corpus (produce the person detained), mandamus (a command to perform a public duty), prohibition (stops a lower court from exceeding jurisdiction), certiorari (quashes an order of a lower court or tribunal) and quo warranto (asks by what authority a person holds a public office). Parliament can make the right to move the courts unavailable only as the Constitution provides, such as during a national emergency under Article 359.
concepts.example: A writ of habeas corpus can be filed if a person is held without lawful authority.

questions.q: The Supreme Court can issue writs to enforce fundamental rights under Article ____.
How many kinds of writs are there?
questions.a: Five

questions.q: The writ that asks the court to produce a detained person is
questions.a: habeas corpus

questions.q: High Courts issue writs under
questions.a: Article 226

questions.q: What does the writ of mandamus do?
questions.a: It commands an official to perform a public duty
o: It commands an official to perform a public duty

questions.q: The writ of quo warranto asks by what ____ a person holds a public office.
questions.a: authority

questions.q: Article 226 differs from Article 32 because it
questions.a: can be used for purposes beyond fundamental rights
o: can be used for purposes beyond fundamental rights

questions.q: Why did Dr Ambedkar call Article 32 the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution?
questions.a: Without a remedy the rights would be only promises
o: Without a remedy the rights would be only promises
It fixes the number of judges

questions.q: The writ of certiorari is used to
questions.a: quash an order of a lower court or tribunal
o: quash an order of a lower court or tribunal

questions.q: A person is detained without a lawful reason. Which writ will the court most likely issue?
questions.a: Habeas corpus

questions.q: A citizen challenges a person holding a public office without qualifications. Which writ fits?
questions.a: Quo warranto

questions.q: A tribunal is about to decide a case outside its powers. Which writ can stop it and what does the writ do?
questions.a: Prohibition, which stops a lower court or tribunal from exceeding its jurisdiction.

questions.q: A municipal officer refuses to issue a birth certificate that the law requires him to issue. Which writ can compel him, and why?
questions.a: Mandamus, since it commands a public officer to perform a legal duty.

questions.q: A person wants to enforce a legal right other than a fundamental right against a State body. The most suitable court is
questions.a: the High Court under Article 226
o: the Supreme Court under Article 32 only

questions.q: Explain why a person may choose the High Court instead of the Supreme Court for a rights violation.
questions.a: Article 226 lets the High Court act for fundamental rights and other legal rights and it is closer and easier to reach, though the citizen may also go to the Supreme Court under Article 32.

questions.q: How is prohibition different from certiorari?
questions.a: Prohibition stops a lower court in advance; certiorari quashes an order already made
o: Prohibition stops a lower court in advance; certiorari quashes an order already made
Prohibition is only for the Army

questions.q: Compare habeas corpus and mandamus.
questions.a: Habeas corpus protects personal liberty by bringing the detained person before the court, while mandamus compels a public authority to do a duty it must do.

questions.q: Why is a remedy as important as a right in a constitutional system?
questions.a: A right without an enforceable remedy is only a statement of intent; writs and courts turn rights into something a citizen can claim.

questions.q: 'Access to courts through writs is the best safeguard of liberty.' Do you agree? Give one reason.
questions.a: A reasoned answer is accepted, such as that independent courts can check the State, though other safeguards also matter.

questions.q: Write a short imaginary petition to a High Court asking for habeas corpus for a detained friend.
questions.a: A petition naming the court, the friend, the detention, the ground that it lacks lawful authority and the relief requested.

concepts.name: Limits, emergencies and landmark ideas about rights
concepts.description: Reasonable restrictions, armed forces, the effect of an emergency, the amendment power and the basic structure idea.
concepts.idea: Rights can be limited and amended, but the Supreme Court has held that the basic structure cannot be destroyed.
concepts.rule: Rights come with reasonable restrictions. Article 33 lets Parliament modify these rights for members of the armed forces and similar services. During a national emergency the rights under Article 19 are suspended when the emergency is declared on the ground of war or external aggression, and the President can suspend the right to move the courts for the enforcement of other rights under Article 359; after the 44th Amendment the rights under Articles 20 and 21 cannot be suspended. Article 368 gives Parliament the power to amend the Constitution. In Golaknath (1967) the Supreme Court held that Parliament could not amend fundamental rights, but in Kesavananda Bharati (1973) it held that Parliament can amend the Constitution but cannot change its basic structure.
concepts.example: Article 21 remains available even during an emergency.

questions.q: The power of Parliament to amend the Constitution is in Article ____.
The case that laid down the basic structure doctrine is
questions.a: Kesavananda Bharati (1973)

questions.q: Rights that cannot be suspended even in an emergency are
questions.a: Article 20 and Article 21

questions.q: Article 33 allows Parliament to modify rights for
questions.a: members of the armed forces
o: the judges of the Supreme Court

questions.q: What does 'basic structure' mean in constitutional law?
questions.a: Core features that Parliament cannot destroy by amendment
o: Core features that Parliament cannot destroy by amendment
The building of the Supreme Court

questions.q: After the 44th Amendment, Articles 20 and 21 cannot be ____ during an emergency.
questions.a: suspended

questions.q: Why does the Constitution allow amendments?
questions.a: A living document must adapt to changing needs
o: A living document must adapt to changing needs
It wants to hide old provisions

questions.q: How did Kesavananda Bharati change the position taken in Golaknath?
questions.a: Parliament could amend rights but not the basic structure
o: Parliament could amend rights but not the basic structure

questions.q: Which statement about Article 359 is correct?
questions.a: It lets the President suspend enforcement of certain rights during an emergency
o: It lets the President suspend enforcement of certain rights during an emergency
It fixes the term of the President

questions.q: A law modifies the rights of soldiers for discipline. It is likely allowed under
questions.a: Article 33

questions.q: A proposed amendment would abolish free elections altogether. According to the basic structure idea, the court is likely to
questions.a: strike it down
o: leave it to the President alone

questions.q: During a national emergency a person is detained. Can he still claim protection of life and personal liberty? Explain.
questions.a: Yes, because after the 44th Amendment Articles 20 and 21 cannot be suspended even during an emergency.

questions.q: Parliament passes an amendment that removes judicial review altogether. How might a court respond using the basic structure idea?
questions.a: It may hold the amendment invalid, because judicial review is regarded as part of the basic structure that cannot be destroyed.

questions.q: A citizen asks whether Parliament can amend a fundamental right at all. The present position is that it
questions.a: can amend, but not destroy the basic structure
o: can amend, but not destroy the basic structure
needs the Prime Minister's consent alone

questions.q: Explain how the Golaknath and Kesavananda Bharati decisions differ on Parliament's amending power.
questions.a: Golaknath held that Parliament could not amend fundamental rights, while Kesavananda Bharati held that it could amend but not alter the basic structure.

questions.q: Why is the basic structure doctrine seen as a balance?
questions.a: It lets the Constitution change while protecting its core
o: It lets the Constitution change while protecting its core

questions.q: Compare the effect of a national emergency on Article 19 and on Articles 20 and 21.
questions.a: Article 19 rights can be suspended when the emergency is on the ground of war or external aggression, but Articles 20 and 21 cannot be suspended after the 44th Amendment.

questions.q: Why do constitutions place some rights beyond suspension even in an emergency?
questions.a: Rights like protection against unfair punishment and against loss of life or liberty are so basic that their loss would allow abuse of power, so they stay even in a crisis.

questions.q: Is it wise to let the courts limit Parliament's amending power? Give one reason.
questions.a: A reasoned answer is accepted, such as that it protects the core of the Constitution against majority overreach.

questions.q: Design a timeline with three landmark events about rights and amendments and one line on each.
questions.a: A timeline with Golaknath (1967), Kesavananda Bharati (1973) and the 44th Amendment (1978), each described in one line.
